title: The Gurus' Muslim friends
hook: Mardana, Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi and Ghani Khan: the story is full of them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women of the early Khalsa, and the name they carry. Your line was kaur means princess. Did you tell a woman who led what she did? Today, the end of the week, and a roll call. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

Mardana. Mian Mir. Budhu Shah. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan. Sher Muhammad Khan of Malerkotla. Rai Kalha of Raikot. Say those names one after another, and something becomes hard to miss. From the first Guru's travels to the tenth Guru's darkest winter, again and again at the turning points of the Sikh story, there's a Muslim friend standing close. Playing the music. Laying a foundation. Sending sons into battle. Carrying the Guru in disguise. Speaking up in court. Opening a door. Today: the Gurus' Muslim friends.
screen: `A ROLL CALL OF NAMES.` → `AT THE TURNING POINTS.` → `A MUSLIM FRIEND STANDING CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning. Mardana, a Muslim musician from Guru Nanak's own village, traveled with him and played the rebab while the Guru sang. Sikh tradition pictures Guru Nanak's hymns reaching people through the two of them together, the song and the strings. Then Mian Mir, the Sufi of Lahore and a friend of Guru Arjan. Tradition credits Mian Mir with laying the foundation stone of the Harmandir. Then Pir Budhu Shah, who sent his sons and followers to fight beside Guru Gobind Singh at Bhangani, where, tradition says, his sons fell. Then the dark winter after Chamkaur: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan carrying the Guru through enemy lines as a holy man, the Nawab of Malerkotla protesting the sentence on the Guru's youngest sons, and Rai Kalha sheltering the Guru and sending for news. And there's a friendship older than any of them, inside the scripture itself. The Guru Granth Sahib holds verses of Sheikh Farid, a Sufi poet, beside the hymns of the Gurus. The Sikh story has real enemies in it: an empire's cruelty, a governor's sentence. But in the way Sikhs tell it, that cruelty never becomes a line drawn around a whole faith, because the friends keep turning up on the Guru's side of it. Now look back at our week. Todar Mal paid gold for the children's cremation. Rai Kalha gave shelter. Mai Bhago led the deserters back. Bhai Mani Singh wrote steadily at Damdama. Bhai Jaita carried the head and was called a son. And the women of the Khalsa took a name that meant they belonged. The Gurus' circle kept widening.
screen: `MARDANA AND THE REBAB.` · `MIAN MIR AND BUDHU SHAH.` · `FRIENDS IN THE DARK WINTER.` · `SHEIKH FARID, INSIDE THE GRANTH.` · then, large: `FRIENDS IN EVERY FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a friend unlike you. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a friend who differs from you in some real way. Another faith, or none. Another country, another generation, another politics. Notice the difference first, plainly, without smoothing it over. Then remember one specific time they stood close anyway: they showed up, they spoke up, they made room. Let that memory be clear and particular. Then find the words of thanks you'd actually send, naming both the difference and the day. The bell holds the time.
The Gurus' Muslim friends. Mardana, Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla, Rai Kalha, and Sheikh Farid inside the scripture itself. Today's word.
Your line: friends in every faith. Today, send that thank-you to the friend you thought of, naming the time they stood close. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana, Mian Mir, Pir Budhu Shah, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla and Rai Kalha with gratitude, and Sheikh Farid's verses are read in the Guru Granth Sahib alongside the Gurus' hymns.

fork.setup: you're telling the Sikh story to a friend. the Gurus faced an empire's cruelty. how do you describe the Muslims in it?
options: as the enemy, all of them.
as people on every side, including close friends.
leave them out of the story.
fork.reveal: the story itself won't draw a line around a whole faith: Mardana, Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi and Ghani Khan, Rai Kalha and more stood close.

notes: Editor pass: 'never lets that turn into a line' softened to 'as Sikhs tell it'; practice reworded to drop 'hold their face' (used day 817) and the repeated Waheguru line.
Week end (days 827–833) look-back is in the teach's last lines.
Mian Mir laying the Harmandir's foundation is given as tradition; historians debate it. Confirm.
The count of Budhu Shah's sons who fell is omitted (the day-817 index says two); confirm.
'Mardana ... from Guru Nanak's own village': tradition (Talwandi); confirm.
Sheikh Farid's shaloks: Ang range 1377–1384 given in sources; confirm. Also Farid's hymns in Asa and Suhi.

Audit pass: ambiguous 'whom tradition credits' (could read as Guru Arjan) split so the foundation claim clearly attaches to Mian Mir; 'the friends are there to see to that' reworded so the narrator doesn't assign the story a purpose.
